title: Jonathan's love (1 Samuel 18:1–4; 20)
hookLine: the king's son gives David his robe and sword, and warns him with arrows
carry: a friend closer than a brother

lines: A ROBE, A SWORD, A BOW, A BELT.
cards: A robe. A sword. A bow.
A belt. The giant is dead, and the shepherd boy who killed him stands before King Saul, still holding the head, answering questions about his father.

Somewhere in that room is the king's son, Jonathan, a soldier himself and the king's heir. And before anyone has worked out what David will mean to this family, Jonathan takes off his own robe and hands it over.
Then his garments. Then his sword, his bow and his belt.

teach.b: Chapter eighteen opens, in the King James Bible: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit, like two threads worked into one cloth.

teach.h: THE HEIR GIVES AWAY HIS ROBE.
teach.b: Then the gift: "Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle." A prince's robe. A prince's weapons.
Some readers see the heir quietly handing his rival the signs of the throne, long before anyone says it out loud. Then the friendship is tested.

Saul wants David dead, and Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend. In chapter twenty they set up a signal. Jonathan will go to a field to practice with his bow, with a boy to fetch the arrows.
If he calls that the arrows are on this side, David is safe. If they are beyond, David must run. The day comes.

teach.h: IS NOT THE ARROW BEYOND THEE?
teach.b: Jonathan shoots and calls out: "Is not the arrow beyond thee?" It's a warning, and a goodbye. When the boy has gone, David comes out of hiding; they kiss one another and weep, and David weeps the most.
Jonathan sends him off in peace, with the promise they made in the name of the Lord, binding them and their children after them.

teach.h: A FRIEND CLOSER THAN A BROTHER.
teach.b: Proverbs has a line that fits: "there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother." Some Christians who teach on friendship turn to these two: a friendship that cost something.

how: Some Christians point to David and Jonathan as a picture of loyal friendship, and the story is read in sermons and small groups about friendship, loyalty and keeping promises.

o: a father's love for the son who would be king
a soldier's love for the king he served in battle
a prince's loyal friendship that cost him something

games.q: Jonathan and David — tap the pairs.
p: how their two souls were joined

s: Jonathan gave David only his robe
he gave his robe, his garments, his sword, his bow and his belt (1 Samuel 18:4).
the arrows were a secret signal
if the arrows were beyond the boy, David had to flee (1 Samuel 20).
the line about a friend closer than a brother is from Proverbs
Proverbs 18:24: a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.

games.q: you're Jonathan. your father, the king, wants your best friend dead. you've promised to warn him. what do you do?
o: side with your father and say nothing.
go to the field and send the signal with your arrows.
games.why: he goes out with his bow and a boy, and calls: "Is not the arrow beyond thee?" then the two friends weep and part in peace.

practice: Bring to mind one friend who has stood with you when it cost them, and stay with their face for a moment.
Then choose one thing that's really yours to give them, not leftovers: a book you love, an hour of your time, a word of thanks you've never said.
If you pray, hold that friend before God in silence; if not, simply think of them with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Jonathan's love. The king's son, knit to David soul to soul, who gave away his robe and sword and warned his friend with an arrow.

orig.note: Hebrew: soul, life, self. Jonathan loved David as his own nefesh (1 Samuel 18:1).

carryVoice: Your line: a friend closer than a brother. Two souls, knit together, and a promise that reached their children. See you tomorrow.
